tools.name: SubagentHandback
tools.description:
Deliver your final report to the agent that spawned you (your caller). Use it once, for that hand-off only: when your work is complete, call SubagentHandback({message: <your full report>}). The call ends your run, so do everything else first and put everything your caller needs in that one report. It is not a messaging channel: do not use it for progress updates or questions.

content.content:
# Fortress microgpt: concurrency and memory handover

As of 2026-11-18 · Pavol Vaškovič

## Purpose

This is context for a Claude Code session working in the Fortress revival repo (github.com/palimondo/fortress). The goal is to make Karpathy's microgpt run fast in Fortress on a multi-core machine (Apple Silicon).

The conclusion of the discussion: keep STM (`atomic`) off the hot path entirely. A GPT training step is dense numeric work with no shared symbolic state. The fitting design is write-once flat arrays in a per-step arena, disjoint-write parallel loops, and a monoid reduction of gradients across the batch.

The discussion was conceptual. Nobody read the Fortress source during it. Every statement about what the Fortress implementation does is an assumption to check, listed under Open questions.

## STM background

STM gives atomicity and isolation for a block of code without locks. It never went mainstream; it works where mutation is already controlled.

**Mechanism (optimistic design).** Each shared variable has a version. A transaction logs its reads (variable + version) and buffers its writes privately. At commit it locks the written variables, checks that no read version changed, then publishes or discards and retries. The alternative writes in place and keeps an undo log. It is the database technique of optimistic concurrency control, without durability.

**Where it works**

- Haskell: the type system bans I/O inside transactions. Idiomatic and used in production.
- Clojure: multiversion STM over explicit `ref` cells that hold immutable values. Only ref operations are instrumented, and writing a ref outside a transaction throws. Rarely used in practice; atoms (one cell, CAS retry) cover most code.

**Why it failed elsewhere** (Microsoft STM.NET cancelled 2010, C++ TM never standardised, PyPy-STM abandoned, Intel TSX disabled)

- I/O cannot roll back, and unrestricted languages cannot forbid it inside a transaction.
- Instrumenting every read and write costs 2–10× single-threaded.
- Weak vs. strong atomicity: code outside transactions touching the same data breaks isolation; fixing it means instrumenting all code.
- Privatisation: removing an object from a shared structure in a transaction, then using it unsynchronised, was unsafe under the fast implementations.
- Joe Duffy's conclusion: the root problem is unrestricted shared mutable state. Get isolation and immutability first; transactions then serve the small remainder.

The selling point was composability (two atomic blocks nest into one; two lock-based components do not compose), not raw speed against hand-tuned locking.

## Fortress specifics

Fortress supports an immutable, reduction-based style in which `atomic` is rarely needed. All of this is from general knowledge of the language, not from the repo.

**STM in Fortress.** The original interpreter implemented `atomic` on a Java STM library derived from DSTM2 (Sun's Scalable Synchronization group), with threads on Doug Lea's fork/join pool. It ran, but no published result shows a multicore gain from it. The bet was on hardware TM in Sun's Rock processor, cancelled in 2009.

**Immutable by default**

- `x = e` is an immutable binding; mutable needs `var` or `:=`.
- Object fields are immutable unless declared `var` or `settable`.
- `value object` gives immutable value types.
- Arrays are mutable.

**Why `atomic` appears.** Fortress is implicitly parallel: `for` bodies, tuple elements and function arguments may run in parallel. A shared accumulator therefore needs it:

```
for i <- 1:n do atomic sum += a[i] end
```

**The intended replacement** is a reduction over a generator, which splits the range, reduces the pieces in parallel and combines them with no shared variable:

```
sum = SUM[i <- 1:n] a[i]
```

**Other escapes**

- `seq(1:n)` forces a sequential loop, where a local `var` accumulator is safe.
- Disjoint array writes (each iteration writes its own `a[i]`) need no `atomic`.

**Strong-atomicity caveat.** The spec makes `atomic` atomic with respect to all other threads. An implementation may therefore route every mutable variable access through the STM, not only accesses inside `atomic` blocks. If this one does, the cost follows `var`, and removing `atomic` blocks alone will not remove it.

## Ideas considered and set aside

These are sound techniques for shared symbolic state. microgpt has none, so none of them is on the path.

| Idea | What it is | Why not here |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Persistent collections (Clojure) | Immutable wide trees; an update copies one root-to-leaf path and shares the rest; one mutable root pointer updated by CAS | Pointer chasing and allocation; nobody does dense linear algebra on persistent vectors |
| Swift-style copy-on-write | In-place mutation when the buffer is uniquely referenced, full copy otherwise | Needs a reference count; the JVM has none. JVM substitutes: ownership tokens (Clojure transients), static uniqueness proof, compiler-inserted counting, or a sticky one-bit "shared" flag |
| Concurrent tries (Ctrie) | Per-node CAS with O(1) snapshots | For write-heavy shared maps, not tensors |
| Off-heap memory (Agrona, `Unsafe`) | Byte-oriented buffers outside the GC heap | `double[]`/`float[]` are already flat and unscanned by the GC, and HotSpot optimises them better than `Unsafe` access |
| LMAX Disruptor | Preallocated ring buffer, single writer, cache-line padding | A messaging structure; only its discipline transfers |

**What does transfer** from the Disruptor school: allocate once, keep data flat, one writer per region, no garbage on the hot path.

**Copy-on-write is unnecessary** because ownership is statically obvious in a training step. Activations are write-once. Only parameters and optimizer state outlive the step, and after the update nobody needs the old values, so they are updated in place.

## Design direction for microgpt

Treat the training step as a pure function over write-once flat arrays, and parallelise across training examples.

**Memory**

- Replace the scalar autograd graph (one heap object per scalar, linked by pointers) with a tape in flat parallel arrays: values, gradients, opcodes, operand indices.
- Allocate the tape once. Reset it each step by resetting an index. This is arena allocation.
- Parameters and optimizer state live in one uniquely owned block, updated in place between steps.

**Parallelism**

- Split loops so each task writes its own slice. Disjoint writes need no `atomic`.
- The hazard is the backward pass, where several consumers add into the same gradient cell. At scalar granularity that is a shared accumulator. At tensor granularity (matmul backward as one operation) it is disjoint-write loops again.
- The matrices are tiny, so threading inside one multiply will lose to scheduling overhead.
- Parallelism pays across examples: map over the batch, reduce per-example gradients with vector addition as the monoid. This is the generator/reducer pattern. The original is believed to train on one document per step, so this adds batching, a benign change to the algorithm.

**GEMM**

- Across cores, each output row or row block is independent, so associativity is not involved.
- Inside a core, the inner dot product is a reduction; strict IEEE ordering blocks SIMD. Declaring `+` associative licenses multiple accumulators and vector lanes.
- Loop order i-k-j makes the inner loop `C[i,:] += A[i,k] * B[k,:]`, which is elementwise and vectorises under strict IEEE.

**Numerics**

- Relaxed reduction order is normal in LLM training: GPU kernels reduce nondeterministically and runs are not bit-reproducible.
- Relax associativity only. Do not assume away NaN and infinity; that hides divergence.
- Keep long accumulations (loss sums, gradient sums over many examples) in higher precision.
- Prefer `float` over `double` where possible: on 128-bit NEON it doubles the lane count.

## JVM tooling status

On JDK 25, primitive arrays plus the incubating Vector API are what is available; value classes are not.

| Tool | Status | Note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Primitive arrays (`double[]`, `float[]`) | Stable | Flat, unboxed, not scanned by the GC. The default choice |
| Vector API (`jdk.incubator.vector`) | Tenth incubator in JDK 25 ([JEP 508](https://openjdk.org/jeps/508)) | Needs `--add-modules jdk.incubator.vector` at compile and run time. Package will be renamed on leaving incubation |
| Foreign Function & Memory API (`MemorySegment`, `Arena`) | Final | Supported replacement for `Unsafe` memory access. Worth it only to hand memory to native BLAS |
| Value classes ([Project Valhalla](https://openjdk.org/projects/valhalla/), JEP 401) | Preview in JDK 28, due March 2027; early-access builds exist | Not in JDK 25. Needs `--enable-preview`. Expected to stay in preview through JDK 29 |

**Vector API discipline.** A vector is an ordinary heap object today. Speed depends on the C2 compiler proving it never escapes. Keep vectors as local variables inside the hot loop, load from and store to primitive arrays, and never put a vector in a field or collection. Otherwise each operation allocates.

**Why the Vector API waits for Valhalla.** Value classes let the VM keep vectors in registers as a property of the type instead of an optimisation that may fail. Finalising the API before that would freeze a shape that then has to break.

**Where Valhalla would matter here.** Only if a Fortress value object (a dual number for autograd, say) should live flat inside an array.

Not verified: the JEP 401 page returned a stale copy when fetched, so the Valhalla status rests on the project page and August 2026 press coverage.

## Open questions to check in the source

These decide whether the design above is reachable in pure Fortress or needs a Java-side native type.

- [ ] Does an array of `RR64` (or `RR32`) compile to a flat primitive array, or to boxed objects?
- [ ] Does mutable variable access outside `atomic` go through the STM (strong atomicity), or only access inside `atomic` blocks?
- [ ] Which standard library paths (array and aggregate internals, generators, reducers) use `atomic` or transactional cells internally?
- [ ] Does the big-operator machinery treat `+` on floats as associative, and how are the `Associative` and `Commutative` traits consulted by reducers?
- [ ] Does a disjoint-write parallel `for` over array indices run without any transactional overhead?
- [ ] How are native Java-implemented types exposed to Fortress in this tree, and can a thin wrapper over `float[]` be added that way?
- [ ] Does microgpt as ported train on one document per step, and where would batching go?
- [ ] Does HotSpot auto-vectorise the i-k-j GEMM inner loop as emitted by the Fortress compiler, or is an explicit Vector API kernel needed?

If arrays box or `var` access is transactional, the fallback is a Java-implemented tensor type (flat array, arena, GEMM kernel) exposed to Fortress, with Fortress supplying the batch-level map and reduce.

## References

**Steele, "Organizing Functional Code for Parallel Execution; or, foldl and foldr Considered Slightly Harmful" (ICFP 2009)** — the design rationale for generators and reducers.

- Video: https://vimeo.com/6624203 (live)
- Slides, MIT version, April 2009, 65 slides: http://groups.csail.mit.edu/mac/users/gjs/6.945/readings/MITApril2009Steele.pdf (live)
- Slides, ICFP version: `research.sun.com/projects/plrg/Publications/ICFPAugust2009Steele.pdf` (dead host; try the Wayback Machine)
- Proceedings abstract, 2 pages, no full paper: DOI 10.1145/1596550.1596551
- Maessen's follow-up talk, Portland State, January 2010: `research.sun.com/projects/plrg/Publications/PSUJan2010-Maessen.pdf` (dead host)

**Pages opened during the discussion**

- JEP 508: Vector API (Tenth Incubator): https://openjdk.org/jeps/508
- Project Valhalla: https://openjdk.org/projects/valhalla/

**Cited from general knowledge, not opened**

- Joe Duffy, "A (brief) retrospective on transactional memory" (2010)
- Dan Grossman, "The Transactional Memory / Garbage Collection Analogy" (2007)
- Harris, Marlow, Peyton Jones, Herlihy, "Composable Memory Transactions" (2005)
- Okasaki, *Purely Functional Data Structures* (1998)
- Bagwell, hash array mapped tries (2001); Steindorfer and Vinju, CHAMP (2015)
- Prokopec et al., concurrent tries with snapshots (2012)
- Tofte and Talpin, region-based memory management

content.content:
Each entry is one line that starts with its permanent number: `F-87` in FACTS, `P-48` in POSITIONS. A FACTS entry is the fact as it stands now, what it means for the work, and the test that fails if the fact stops holding, under a bold title. If no test checks the fact, the entry gives the command and the output that show it. It points to the report section that holds the detail. Cite an entry by its number. If the reader must know what the entry says without printing it, add the first words of its title in quotes: F-87, "The first words ...".

## The gap ledger

The ledger's rows are the bug reports that the work fixes. A fix of a row starts with its reproduction, written as a test (`tests-writing.md`).

A row is one line of eight cells, at most 1,200 characters, in the table of a topic section. Reports cite a row by its number, which it keeps for good. A new issue gets a new row.

- Its status is one of seven words: `POSITIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-BOUNDED`, `CONTESTED`, `RETIRED`, `FIXED`, `DUPLICATE`. The last three close a row. The row template (below) defines each.
- Its class is a kind and an area, such as `implementation gap (checker)`.
- The earlier text of a changed row is in `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger-history.md`.

Read the ledger only through the queries below: it is too large to read whole.

A row states its gap as it stands now. A note adds a fact. If your work changes what a row says, write the row's whole new line with `rewrite` (below), not a note that tells the repair.

The heading reader of `ledger.py` does not expand the specification's `\Trait{X}` macro. So a row that names a library trait's section cites `Specification-1.0-frozen/` by line.

## Reading the record

Read only the slice of the record that you need. This tool prints whole entries, in parts of bounded size:

    T=explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh

- `$T 'F-87'` prints one entry by its number, and `$T 'P-48'` one of POSITIONS. `$T 'F-87+'` adds each entry that F-87 cites by its number, and each entry that cites F-87. `$T 'history:F-87'` prints its history. Run one when your brief or a note cites an entry by its number.
- `$T 'positions:WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints one of the curator's decisions. Run it before you choose among ways to do something. If several titles hold the words, it names them.
- `$T 'WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints each FACTS entry whose bold title holds them, and `$T 'section:HEADING'` every entry of a FACTS section. Run one before you investigate a behaviour of the tree, and when your brief or a note names an entry. These queries and `positions:` read titles only: before you write that the record does not hold something, also grep FACTS and POSITIONS for its words.
- `$T 'index:WORDS'` prints the INDEX lines that hold the words. Run it to find the notes on a topic.
- `$T 'ledger-find:WORDS'` prints one line for each ledger row that holds every word. Run it when you meet a defect, before you investigate it.
- `$T 'ledger:ROW'` prints one row whole. Run it for each row that you need from a find, your brief or a note.
- `$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'` prints a section of any note, or of a `.tex` chapter, and `$T 'map:FILE#HEADING'` a section of a note under `explorations/coordinator/map/`. Run one when your brief or a note names a section. `#HEADING@WORDS` prints only the table rows and list items of that section that hold every one of WORDS.
- `$T --check QUERY ...` prints only where each query matches and its size. Run it before a query whose size you do not know. `--part N` prints part N of a long output, and `--help` gives the rest.

A word of a query that ends in `*` matches the start of a word. Any other word matches a whole word.

Before you edit a file of the original tree, list the ledger rows that cite it, and read each row that your edit can change:

    python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py find --cites FILE

## Writing to the record

- Write FACTS and POSITIONS only with `explorations/coordinator/tools/record.py`, never by hand. `add` gives a new entry its number, and `set` rewrites an entry. The tool writes the entry to `FACTS.md` or `POSITIONS.md`, and its earlier text to the history file beside it. It commits nothing: commit both files in one commit. Its header gives its usage.
- If your brief lets you write FACTS, add each fact as a new entry in the section of its topic, in the commit that establishes it. Put its detail in a section of your report: the file:line citations, the commands with their output, and the measured numbers. Point the entry to that section, by your report's file and the section's heading. If your report is only your final message, hand the fact over instead. Spend no effort on the entry's wording: it is rewritten to the record's form after your work.
- If your brief does not let you write FACTS, hand each fact over in the "For FACTS" item of your report, with:
  - the fact as it stands now, in one sentence;
  - what it means for the work;
  - the number that a decision rests on, if any, with what it counts; if its parts belong to different ledger rows, the part of each row;
  - the test that fails if the fact stops holding, or the command and the output that show it;
  - the section of your report that holds the detail.
- If your brief lets you write FACTS, rewrite a wrong entry in place. Otherwise say in your hand-over that the entry is wrong, with the evidence.
- POSITIONS holds each of the curator's decisions, in one place. Everything else points there. Write a decision there only if your brief gives it to you to record. If you have evidence against one, do as `exploring.md` says.
- Put new files of the work under `explorations/`. If you add a note directly in `explorations/` or `explorations/reviews/`, add its line to INDEX: ``- `PATH`: `` and the first sentence of the note's header comment.

Write the gap ledger only with `ledger.py`, which checks each line that it writes against the row template.

    L="python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py"

To add a row:

1. Print the row template, about 3 KB: `$T 'doc:explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md#The row template'`.
2. Write the row as one line in a file under your tree's `tmp/`, with `?` in its number cell.
3. Run `$L add FILE --section TITLE`. It numbers the row and puts it in that section. If the row breaks the template, it adds nothing and prints each rule broken. `$L sections` lists the titles.

To change a row:

- `$L note N TEXT` adds TEXT to the notes of row N. It refuses a note that takes the row past 1,200 characters, or its notes cell past 700 characters. `$L note N TEXT --check` writes nothing. It says whether TEXT fits, and how many characters the notes and the row have left now and would have left with TEXT. These counts include the separator that the tool adds. It exits 0 if TEXT fits, and 1 if not. Run it before a long note, or before a note on a row near its limits. If TEXT does not fit, shorten it, or cut the notes with `rewrite` (below).
- `$L rewrite N FILE` replaces row N with the whole line in FILE, a file under your tree's `tmp/`, with N or `?` in its number cell. Use it to correct the claim, cut the notes or change the reproducer. The tool checks the line against the template and keeps the old line in the history file.
- `$L duplicate N --of M` makes row N a pointer to row M.
- `$L close N --commit HASH --test NAME` marks row N `FIXED`, by the commit HASH and its test NAME. Run it once that commit is in `HEAD`, and commit the close after it. NAME can also be a file under `explorations/coordinator/tools/`, or `none` with `--note REASON`. For a `CONTESTED` row, add `--settled TEXT`, which names what settled its question.
- `$L landing-check BASE` prints each problem, and exits 1 on any. Run it when your brief asks for it. It checks the whole ledger against the template, so a broken row that BASE already had counts too. The problems are a row that breaks the template, an `XXX` test deleted or renamed while a row that is not closed names it, a row that is not closed though a commit says it fixed it, and a FACTS or POSITIONS entry that disagrees with a row's status.

## The repository's history

- The repository is a 2018 fork of `sirinath/fortress`, a git conversion of the project's java.net Mercurial repository. Its trunk runs from 2007-01-04 to 2012-08-31 and ends at `a874948ac`, the team's last commit.
- The commits after `a874948ac` are the revival's. After the tag `sealed-tree`, commit `75cca6683`, the revival began to fix the team's code, test first. Before it, the revival changed mainly the build and the toolchain.
- `git diff a874948ac -- FILE` shows what the revival changed in a file, and `git diff 75cca6683 -- FILE` what it changed after the tag.
- If the commands above fail, run `git rev-parse --is-shallow-repository`. It prints `true` in a shallow clone, where these commits do not resolve. There, a copyright header of Sun Microsystems or Oracle, as in `Library/Format.fss`, marks a file that the team made, but not which of its lines the port or the revival changed. If your task needs those lines, say in your report that the clone is shallow.
- The conversion cut 146 parent links, so a `git log` of a directory stops at a cut and misses the team's earlier commits. Use `git log --follow` on a file, or compare contents.
- To find who wrote something, or where the repository's history after 2012 comes from, read `research/authorship.md` and `explorations/coordinator/lineage.md`.
- Commit `8fe1daa8f` copied a third-party port of the tree to Java 9 onto the team's last commit, `a874948ac`. Give its lines no credit, and name no author of it in any text that you commit. In a reconstruction of authorship, attribute nothing of it to anyone.

## The principle for the batches

Every batch lands with the specification, the library and both paths agreeing. So the work is grouped by what has to change together, not split finer.

Two rules of the batch machinery shape the order: two rungs in one batch may not change the same declaration, and a rung cannot build on another rung of its own batch, since every rung branches from the batch's base (`coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.js:1303`, batch rule 1).

Its cost is not measured (F-385; `reviews/batch-33-review.md`, section 2, Q2, and "Findings for the record").
- The library's own splits: the matrix product `mul` and the strided ranges still split down to one element. In a Java model of the model's step in the library's fork/join shape, that costs 19 to 80 times at the library's grains, and 1.4 to 4.8 times with the product stopped at blocks of 16 (F-356; `reviews/plan-review-2026-11-10.md`, section 6.2, line 6). Whether `mul` gets a grain now or with the first compiled kernel is review-queue item 523.

- F-11 **The code generator boxes every number, and boxing is the main representational cost of microGPT-shaped array code.** So a compiled `RR64` loop holds no `dadd` or `dmul` (the `fortress-repo` skill, "The compiled runtime"). In Java models of microGPT's three kernels, boxed elements cost 6.3× (dot product), 6.5× (matrix product) and 2.6× (row lift) over `double[]`. No such kernel compiles yet: the compiler prelude has no array type (row 305), and the arrays reach the compiled path with the one library (P-37). In a hot compiled loop, escape analysis removes the temporary boxes, and one box per assignment to a mutable variable per iteration stays (F-301), as long as C2's inline depth reaches each box's constructor chain (F-302). Detail: `perf-probes/kernels/REPORT.md` sections 2 and 4; `perf-probes/helper-calls/REPORT.md` section 4.

FACTS.md:12
- F-18 **On the compiled path, the class loader makes the class of a generic instantiation at its first use, by rewriting the template's bytecode with ASM, and the rewriting only renames, so it gives no instance a `double[]` field.** The class is `InstantiatingClassloader`; the `fortress-repo` skill's "The compiled runtime" gives the mechanism. A size is part of the made class's name, as in `pNatMeth$Box⟦3⟧`, the object `Box` at size 3 in the probe component `pNatMeth`. Inside the class, the size's descriptor is `RTTIsize.of("<n>")` (F-129). A field of the template's type `T`, `LT;`, becomes `LFRR64;` in `Box⟦FRR64⟧`, and `[D` is no class name, so stamping alone keeps every number boxed (F-11). The team left two separate traces for unboxing. The plan in `compiler/optimization/Unbox.java` lists what to unbox: a primitive, a singleton object, unboxed fields, and a `comprises` clause whose types are unboxable; it says nothing of the loader or of instantiations. The loader has an empty "expando" stub (`runtimeSystem/InstantiatingClassloader.java:168-172`). A loader that stamps an `RR64` instance with a `double[]` field, way A4 of array decision A (P-85), does not exist and is unmeasured. Walk instantiates generics in its own evaluator, not by classes. == explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md, ## The goal

POSITIONS.md:7
- P-7 **The goal is to finish what the designers intended, measured by one program, microGPT, compiled to JVM bytecode and running fast.** The revival judges what the designers intended by the team's own sources: its Working Draft of February 2011, its texts on types and its code. `Specification/` holds the Working Draft as a living document: the revival revises it and states each change (P-95). The texts on types include the Types chapter of the specification's 2012 restart (P-25). In `Papers/`, they include the OOPSLA 2011 paper, Naden's 2012 write-up and the POPL 2019 paper with its technical report. P-26 says when code counts, and which source wins where two conflict. The revival does not redesign the language. A pure-Java microGPT is the baseline that compiled microGPT is measured against: the optimal result, the one to aim at.

POSITIONS.md:9
- P-9 **The revival searches for the most readable expression of the microGPT algorithm.** C4 is the flat microGPT program (`explorations/run-c4/src/MicroGptFlat.fss`), whose data layout follows Aaron Hsu's flat style of APL (P-29: C4 is not edited for speed before microGPT runs compiled). In C4, the polishing happens in the vocabulary, the array operations that the model's lines call: `FlatArrays.fss` beside C4, and what of it has moved into the standard library (P-27: what a program builds that a more mature library would hold goes into the library). P-87 holds the limit: the model's text is the notation, and a change to a model line is shown to the curator as a diff first. C4 is the target form of the APL microGPT program (`explorations/apl/mg/MicroGptApl.fss`): the APL program is written so that each of its lines expands into the line that C4 writes by hand. C4 writes its hyperparameters as tuple bindings, such as `(nEmbd, blockSize, nHead, headDim, vocabSize, bosId) = (16, 16, 4, 4, 27, 26)`, the form to which the APL sub-language (P-10) expands a strand assignment, APL's binding of several names at once. The one-line form, declarations separated by semicolons such as `nEmbd = 16; blockSize = 16; ...`, is not used: the APL sub-language has no use for it.

== explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md, ## Decisions on record, ### Arrays and the model program

POSITIONS.md:111
- P-84 **On the compiled path, the array of every number type is to be stored unboxed, in a Java array of its primitive type, and every array is to have the most efficient store that its element type allows; arrays keep the team's `nat` sizes in their types.** `RR64` goes in a `double[]`, `ZZ32` in an `int[]`, and so on, for each number type that has a Java primitive type; `RR64`'s `double[]`, the model's, is the first case. Why: a high-performance language cannot box its array elements, and the sizes are central to the team's design. So the storage and the sizes are one design: the sizes stay in the array types as `nat` static parameters, as the library's `Vector` and `Matrix` declare them, and the compiled checker checks them. The sizes do not wait while a first version of the store carries them only as run-time fields; that layered plan was rejected. Both halves follow the library's own patterns (P-27, on extending the library in its own way). The compiled checker checks `nat` static parameters (F-67). The class loader, as it makes a generic instance's class, only renames the type parameter, so it gives no instance a `double[]` field; a loader that would, way A4 of array decision A (P-85), is unmeasured (F-18).

POSITIONS.md:112
- P-85 **The array design's three questions are open, with no default, and return after the switch-over with the array decisions A, B and D.** The array design is the compiled path's design for arrays. The three questions: how the array factory chooses the store of each element type; whether the store also keeps the size as a field, beside the size in the type; and whether a factory for a size known only at run time returns the unsized `Array[\E,I\]`, whose type holds no size. These questions are apart from decisions A, B and D: decision A is how an array of a number type, made through the library's generic array traits, gets its unboxed store, `RR64`'s `double[]` first (P-84); B is where unboxed arithmetic happens; and D is the sizes in the model's own types (P-87). The whole preparation for the array work is to be done before the switch-over; only the work itself waits.

POSITIONS.md:113
- P-87 **The model's text is the notation, and the vocabulary is repaired around it.** The model is microGPT's two programs; the vocabulary is the array operations that they are written in (`FlatArrays.fss` for C4, the flat program, and `FlatArrays2.fss` for the APL-style one). No operator in the model is replaced by a function call to pass an overload check, as a proposed repair once wrote `planeSum(mask, x)` for `mask + x`; the vocabulary changes instead. Any repair that changes a line of the model is shown to the curator as a diff before it is built. Decision D, still open and returning after the switch-over with the other array decisions (P-85), is such a diff: it gives C4's arrays sized types, in its vocabulary's signatures and in the model lines that these force (`explorations/reviews/decision-d-diff.md`; the patch itself is only in git, in the parent of `84aef6a4f`). == explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md, ## Decisions on record, ### Numbers

POSITIONS.md:97
- P-159 **A float compared with a NaN answers: `<`, `<=`, `>` and `>=` give `false`, and `CMP` gives `Unordered`, on both paths.** On `RR64` and `RR32` the four ordering operators answer `false` when either side is a NaN, and `CMP` answers `Unordered`, as the team built them. `FloatingComparisonError` stays declared in both libraries, and nothing raises it. The specification's overview of operators said that this comparison threw that error, and the sentence before it that a rational comparison at 1/0 or 0/0 threw `RationalComparisonError` (`Specification/basic/operators/opr-overview.tex:283-288`). Both sentences are revised, in the form of Appendix I, to the rationals chapter's reading: 0/0 compares `false` "for compatibility with floating-point arithmetic", and the infinities are ordered (F-319). Row 672 closed with that edit. Why: a NaN test in software would slow the comparison against the hardware's own; measured, it is noise on today's boxed compiled path and costs 15 to 20 percent a comparison on unboxed doubles in Java, and whether it stops vectorisation is open (`perf-probes/nan-check-cost/REPORT.md`). The team built `false` and `Unordered` everywhere and never raised the error, and Java, Swift, Python's floats, Julia and Haskell all answer `false`.

POSITIONS.md:31
- P-175 **On the compiled path a call's arguments run in parallel where `ParallelismAnalyzer` judges them worth a task, as a tuple's elements do, so a reduction's two halves run in parallel; the one library's parallel range stops its split at a grain size, not at single elements.** The one library's range joins a reduction's halves as the arguments of one call, `red.join(loop'(lo, mid-1), loop'(mid, hi))`, and split down to single elements when the curator decided (`Library/RangeInternals.fss:1312-1350`); the code generator evaluated a call's arguments in order, under the team's comment "Why isn't this parallel???", so every `SUM`, `DOT` and `BIG MAX` of microGPT would have run its bodies one at a time once compiled programs ran the one library. The split stops at a chunk that runs efficiently in sequence: in his words, "you need the right forking constants", as Steele's parallel trees end in sequential leaves and Clojure's persistent vectors take their branching factor from B-trees. It needs a group of forked arms to join every arm before it completes abruptly, which the compiled path did not do (`CodeGen.genParallelExprs` joined on the normal path only; `reviews/parallelism-foundations-2026-11-08.md`, section 7.1); F-350 gives what it does now. The library binding the halves as a tuple, and reductions left in sequence, are declined. Why: the specification evaluates each argument of a call in an implicit thread of its own (`Specification/basic/evaluation/parallelism.tex:60-64`), walk forks a call's arguments (`interpreter/evaluator/Evaluator.java:342`), and the model's parallelism is its reductions (the review, section 6). Detail: the review, sections 1.8, 6, 7.1 and 8.

# Performance roadmap: two routes from notation to speed

## Where we start (measured)

- The walk interpreter runs the whole language and is about a thousand times slower than Karpathy's pure-Python microGPT on the same workload (`explorations/blinded-fable/notes/`, `explorations/matrix-ad-probes/REPORT.md`).
- The bytecode compiler runs about a tenth of the language and is only 7-9x faster than the interpreter (`explorations/compiled-path-gaps.md`).
- Both paths execute the same object protocol: every `RR64` is a heap object (`FRR64`; the code generator emits no native double arithmetic), every call is symmetric multimethod dispatch on run-time types, generic classes are instantiated at load time, and `for`/`Σ` run as generator closures under the fork-join task runtime.
- The static type checker (Scala, `scala_src/typechecker/`) runs only on the compile path; `walk` leaves it switched off, so the interpreter runs untyped desugared trees and accepts spec-illegal programs (`explorations/libvector-report.md` §0).
- Fortress's `Σ` is defined to combine in generator order, which licenses the reassociation a vectorizer needs; the price is measured at the sixteenth digit (golden checks in all three microGPT runs).
- A bare accumulator in a parallel `for` silently loses updates at four threads; `atomic` or a reduction fixes it (`explorations/matrix-ad-probes/`).

## The thesis to test

Fortress's type system (symmetric multiple dispatch, reified generics, multiple inheritance, modular static checking) has never run at a useful speed. Julia runs three of the four by dropping modular static checking and specializing at run time. Scala runs static resolution plus unboxing and specialization but never had symmetric dispatch. Showing all four together at CPython speed or better, on the JVM, would be new. The driver program is microGPT, gated by the existing golden check (logits, loss, all gradients against the pinned Python).

**Driver program, refined.** Karpathy's scalar `Value` carries a mutable `grad`, so it is a reference object and stays a heap node under any scheme; unboxing helps it little. The matrix-level formulation probed in `explorations/matrix-ad-probes/` (plain `RR64` vectors and matrices, closures composed as the backward tape) is the one that becomes all-primitive under A1/A2 and is therefore the performance driver. The scalar tape can also be made fast by changing its data structure to parallel arrays (`data[]`, `grad[]`, child indices), which is how tape-based autodiff is written in C, and is what flattening a `value object` node into an array yields.

## Phase 0: shared foundation (both routes need it)

0.1 **Type-checked interpreter.** Turn the static checker on for `walk` (`Shell.java`: `walk` sets the Scala checker off and the checking flag defaults false; there is no command-line switch for it today, so one must be added) and catalogue what breaks: the 2012 prelude has never been type-checked, and the interpreter has run spec-illegal programs without complaint. Expected outcomes: a list of prelude fixes, a list of checker gaps (the team's own `not_working_static_tests`, 43 files, is the starting catalogue), and a conforming interpreter. This is prerequisite work for both routes: the compiler route needs static types for every Scala technique below, and the Truffle route needs them for initial specializations and as the conformance gate.

0.2 **Benchmark harness.** microGPT forward, backward and one Adam step at the reference size, plus the two scalar benchmarks from the compiled-path report, timed on interpreter, compiler and CPython, recorded in the tree. Every later step reports against this table.

0.3 **Type-system stress map.** Which specified features were retracted or restricted between the frozen 1.0 spec and the later one, which have no implementation and no test, and which require run-time type information of generic instantiations to specialize. Sources: `Papers/Dispatch`, `Papers/RuntimeInstantiation`, `Papers/Welterweight`, the not-working test directories, `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md`. No backend rescues an unchecked ambiguity. Record separately every `comprises` clause in the prelude: each is closed-world information the 2012 compiler never used for dispatch.

0.4 **Value audit of the library.** The specification distinguishes value objects (immutable fields, no identity, compared by contents; keyword `value`) from reference objects, and the built-in numbers are declared value objects (`value object Float extends RR64`, `Int`, `Boolean`, …). The 2012 code generator gives the modifier no representation meaning. Counted on 2026-09-08: 30 `value object` and 5 `value trait` declarations against 543 `object` and 313 `trait` declarations in `Library/` and `LibraryBuiltin/`, while only six library files declare a `var` field, and the collections are persistent structures (`Map`/`Set` as immutable balanced trees, `PureList` as a finger tree, `List` as an immutable array list with a hand-rolled uniqueness flag for in-place extension). The library is value-semantic in behaviour and reference-typed in declaration. The audit marks every object whose fields are all immutable and whose identity is never observed as `value` (respecting the rule that a value trait's subtypes must be value too), which costs nothing today and supplies the licence A1 and A2 need to unbox, split into fields, and lay out in structure-of-arrays form. Fortress has no ownership, reference counting or uniqueness types; sharing is free because the structures do not mutate, and the rare mutable structure is guarded by `atomic` over the runtime's transactional memory.

## Route A: the compiler, taking what Scala took

Keep the front end (parser, disambiguator, checker, desugarers). Modernize the code generator and the compiler library. Each step is known technique; each is gated by `ant testFast` plus the microGPT golden check.

A1 **Unbox by static type.** Map `RR64`/`ZZ32`/`Boolean` to JVM primitives wherever the checker's type is monomorphic; box only at generic boundaries. Scala's treatment of `Double`. Generalized by 0.4: any `value object` whose fields are primitives is flattened into its fields, in locals as separate slots, in fields of enclosing objects as separate fields, and in arrays as one primitive array per field (structure of arrays), which needs nothing from the VM and is licensed by the absence of identity. A flattened value must be re-boxed at a boundary typed by an unknown `T` or at a call the static types do not decide, so A3 and `comprises` sealing keep the boundaries off the hot path. Single-field value objects, which include every number type, follow the Kotlin/Scala value-class scheme (erasure in monomorphic positions, boxing at generic ones, name mangling to keep the two signatures apart); Fortress's existing mangling in `Naming.java` is extended rather than replaced. No JVM language does compiler-driven structure of arrays; Apache Arrow, Spark's columnar format and ND4J do it by hand as libraries, and ISPC, Jai and Julia's StructArrays do it with compiler cooperation elsewhere.

A2 **Specialized arrays.** `Array1[\RR64,…\]` backed by `double[]`, selected from the element type carried at run time. Scala's `Array[Double]` via class tags. Requires the compiler library to gain generic arrays at all (gap G2).

A3 **Static overload resolution.** Where the checker decides the overload, emit a direct call; the JIT inlines it. Scala does this for every call.

A4 **Dynamic dispatch through `invokedynamic`.** For the calls the static types do not decide, an inline-cached call site over run-time type tags replaces the 2012 generated type-test chains. Behind the call site, one generic run-time dispatcher per operator, on the pattern of Clojure's `MultiFn` (a method table, a best-match search over the subtype relation, a cache keyed by the tuple of argument types, invalidated when a component links in new overloads), with the match relation upgraded to Fortress's type lattice and the call-time ambiguity check dropped because the checker excludes ambiguity statically. This is the one piece Scala never needed and the piece that ate the 2012 team; `invokedynamic` (JDK 7) and default methods on interfaces (JDK 8) arrived after their design was fixed. Where a trait is sealed by `comprises`, the overload set is closed and the dispatcher can be compiled to a direct call or a fixed decision tree (Dylan's sealing, Vortex's class hierarchy analysis).

A5 **Loop lowering.** Recognize a generator over a known range and a known monoid reduction, and emit a sequential counted loop; fork-join only above a size threshold, with the reduction's declared algebra licensing the split. Scala's closure inliner and Java's parallel-stream splitting are the worked examples. This is where bounds-check elimination and SIMD then come free from HotSpot, for floating-point loops only; checked integer arithmetic keeps integer loops scalar until one of the remedies in the corrections below applies.

A6 **Generic reductions in the compiler library** (gaps G1, G4, G3): `Σ`, `BIG MAX`, comprehensions, `exp`/`log`. About 4,000 lines of library over generic traits the builtin layer already declares.

A7 **Raise the emitted classfile version** once the load-time rewriting pipeline maintains stack-map frames.

Order: A6 and A2 unblock microGPT at all; A1, A3, A5 deliver the speed; A4 generalizes; A7 is hygiene.

## Route B: the interpreter on Truffle

Keep the same front end. Rebuild only the evaluator (`interpreter/evaluator/`) as Truffle nodes: one class per AST node kind with specializations, built from the type-checked, desugared tree. Truffle partially evaluates the interpreter against each hot program and hands the residue to Graal, which emits machine code; failed speculations deoptimize and re-specialize.

B1 **Node skeleton for the microGPT subset**: literals, variables, calls, object construction, field access, operator methods, `if`, `for` over ranges, reductions, closures.

B2 **Specializations**: `RR64` as `double`, `ZZ32` as `int`, inline caches on multimethod call sites keyed by run-time type tags, escape analysis to remove boxes.

B3 **Library on the same nodes**: the 2012 prelude runs through the new evaluator unchanged; native functions map onto host interop.

B4 **Parallel loops**: the generator protocol's fork-join under Truffle, with the same size-threshold policy as A5.

B5 **Whole-language coverage**, then retire the 2012 evaluator.

The static checker is not strictly required for Truffle, which specializes on observed run-time types, but it makes first guesses right, keeps guards cheap, and is the only way the interpreter becomes spec-conforming. Phase 0.1 is therefore on the critical path for B as well.

Caveat carried from the backend notes: Truffle wants Graal; the JVM Vector API is intrinsified most reliably by the stock C2 compiler. Within-core SIMD is the one line where Route A on stock HotSpot may hold an advantage. To be re-verified against current releases when reached.

## Reference implementations, by step

Each technique in the routes has a worked example to read before implementing. None of the code should be copied; Clojure in particular is under the Eclipse Public License and this tree is BSD.

- **A1, unboxing by static type.** Scala's treatment of `Double`: object in the language, primitive in the bytecode wherever the static type is known, boxed only at generic boundaries. SBCL shows the same from declared types inside a dynamic language.

- **A2, specialized arrays and reified generics.** Scala's `Array[Double]` chosen through a class tag. The .NET runtime is the existence proof that a JIT VM can hold reified generics with value-type instantiations specialized and reference-type instantiations shared, since 2005; Project Valhalla is the JVM's version of the same and its status must be checked per release. Kotlin's inline functions with reified type parameters are the cheap trick for small generic helpers. Rust monomorphization is the whole-program alternative; Swift's witness tables (type metadata plus per-trait implementation tables passed at run time, one compiled copy of generic code, hot paths specialized by the optimizer) are the separate-compilation alternative that fits the component/API design, and Fortress's run-time type objects in `compiler/runtimeValues/` are half of one already. Zig's compile-time evaluation of types as values is the model for `nat` parameters and size-indexed arrays.

- **A3, static overload resolution.** Every statically typed JVM language; the checker already computes the answer.

- **A4, dynamic multimethod dispatch.** Clojure's `clojure.lang.MultiFn` for the dispatcher shape; C#'s `dynamic` on the Dynamic Language Runtime for call-site binders with polymorphic inline caches (built 2008 to 2010, the same design as `invokedynamic`); Julia's per-call-signature method cache for the specialize-once-per-type-tuple discipline; Chambers's Cecil/Vortex work for class hierarchy analysis and compiled dispatch trees; Dylan's sealing for turning closed overload sets into static calls, which Fortress's `comprises` already expresses.

- **A5, loop lowering.** Scala's `for` desugars to `foreach`/`map`/`flatMap` with a closure per body, exactly as Fortress desugars to `generate`; Scala pays for it with HotSpot inlining of monomorphic closure sites, the Scala 2.12 optimizer's closure inliner, Scala 3 `inline`, and specialized function types. Scala's parallel collections and Java's parallel streams are the cautionary examples for the fork-join side: split only above a size threshold, sequential loop inside each chunk. Fortress adds what neither has, the reduction's declared algebra licensing the split.

- **Route B.** TruffleRuby, GraalPy and Espresso as the reference interpreters; PyPy's meta-tracing as the one genuine sibling of the derive-the-JIT approach.

## Corrections recorded on the way

- **Checked integer arithmetic blocks A5's SIMD claim on integer loops.** Recorded 2026-09-17, after the rung 6 skeptic's overflow finding sent me to read how the compiler world spells `+`.

The compiler world binds `+` on `ZZ32` to `jIntOverflowingAdd` (`LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss:625`), which tests the sign bits and throws `IntegerOverflow`; `BOXPLUS` on the next line is `jIntWrappingAdd`, and a saturating family sits beside both in `nativeHelpers/simpleIntArith.java`. Trapping by default with an explicit wrapping operator is the design Swift shipped two years after this tree stopped, and the spec carries `BOXPLUS` as a ring operator on the integers (`Specification/basic-lib/basic-integers.tex:114-117`), so it is design intent and not an implementation accident. Fortress also has the saturating family, which Swift does not, and its overflow is a catchable exception where Swift's is a hard stop.

The cost is not the test itself, which is two bit operations and a branch that is never taken. The cost is that the branch is a side exit from the loop body, and HotSpot's SuperWord pass vectorizes only counted loops with no control flow inside them, so an integer loop whose body can raise `IntegerOverflow` stays scalar however well it is written.

Scope, stated so this is not read as worse than it is: microGPT's hot arithmetic is `RR64`, and IEEE addition does not trap, so the driver program's inner loops are untouched by this. What it touches is integer work, which is indices, counters, `ZZ32` reductions, and the address arithmetic A2 introduces.

Four ways out, cheapest first, none of them measured yet. Let the JIT's range analysis fold the check away where the loop bounds are known, which is the argument for replacing the hand-written sign test with `Math.addExact`, because C2 has an overflow node for that one that it can reason about and can compile the failure path as an uncommon trap rather than as real code in the loop. Use `BOXPLUS` where the declared algebra or a `nat` bound proves the range cannot be left, which is what the operator exists for. Accumulate in a wider type so overflow is impossible inside the loop and check once on the way out. Drop the check only where the checker proved the bound, never as a default, because the default is the language's promise.

Measure before acting: the claim that the check blocks vectorization is read off HotSpot's documented SuperWord restrictions, not off a disassembly of this tree, and 0.2's harness is where it gets settled.

- The runtime-instantiation notes under `Papers/RuntimeInstantiation` are about when a generic function's type parameters may be instantiated at run time under the return-type rule, a soundness question; they are not an optimization plan. Boxing and unspecialized generics were not on the 2012 team's worklist at all.

- The emitted classfiles stay at version 1.6 because the load-time rewriting pipeline drops stack-map frames and the JVM's bytecode verifier may fall back to type inference only at that version; execution is unaffected. The verifier checks JVM types, never Fortress types, which do not survive into the classfile.

- Fortress is a small language in surface (loops, numbers, arrays and big operators are library) and a large one in kernel (the type rules that make library extension checkable). The cost of the small surface is that the compiler no longer knows what a loop is; A5 is the repair.

## Both routes, or one?

Both is not too ambitious if Phase 0 is shared and the two routes are kept in separate directories: A edits `compiler/codegen/` and the compiler library, B adds a new evaluator package; neither touches the other's code. They share the gate and the benchmark table, so the comparison is fair by construction. The economics differ: Route A is incremental and every step is testable in isolation, which suits delegated workers; Route B has a long silent period before the first program runs end to end, and needs one worker with the whole evaluator in view. Sequencing that respects both: start A1-A3 and A6 as worker-sized steps immediately after Phase 0; start B1 in parallel as a single long-running worker; hold a checkpoint when either route runs the microGPT forward pass, and decide then whether to continue both.

## What would count as success

- microGPT forward+backward+Adam at reference size within 2x of pure CPython on one core, on either route, golden check green.
- The same program at least 2x faster on four cores than on one, from the language's own `for`/`Σ`, with no source changes.
- Every optimization justified by a static type or a declared algebra, never by suppressing the language's semantics (order-independent reductions, implicit parallelism, symmetric dispatch).
- A written account of which of Fortress's four type-system ingredients each route kept, restricted, or deferred, so the thesis is answered honestly whether or not the numbers are reached.

# Execution-backend options for a Fortress revival

Where the speed could come from, if the project ever wants it. Context that frames every option: the 2012 code generator emits the language's object protocol faithfully (boxed numbers, symmetric multimethod dispatch at every call, generic classes instantiated at run time, loop bodies as closures under the task runtime), which is why compiled Fortress is only 7-9x faster than the tree-walking interpreter and roughly a thousand times slower than plain Java on a scalar loop (`explorations/compiled-path-gaps.md`). The front end (Rats! parser, ASTGen node classes, disambiguation, the Scala static checker) is runtime-agnostic and survives any backend choice.

## 1. Truffle on GraalVM (ranked first)

GraalVM is an ordinary JDK whose C2 JIT is replaced by Graal through the JVMCI interface; existing bytecode runs unchanged. Truffle is a Java framework on top of it for implementing languages: write an AST interpreter (a class per node kind, an `execute` method, specialization annotations for the types a node has actually observed) and Truffle partially evaluates that interpreter against each hot program, constant-folding away the interpreter loop, the dispatch and the boxing, and hands the residue to Graal. Speculation failures deoptimize back to the interpreter and re-specialize. TruffleRuby, GraalJS, GraalPy, FastR and Espresso (Java on Truffle) are the reference points.

Fit for this repository: the evaluator layer is rebuilt as Truffle nodes; parser, AST and static checker are reused; native functions map onto host interop. The result still runs on a plain JDK (as an interpreter) and gets specializing compilation when Graal is present. Expected wins: polymorphic inline caches for multimethod dispatch, unboxed numerics through partial escape analysis, generics specialized per instantiation. Cost: a serious port of a large evaluator whose environment-threading style must be reshaped into Truffle idioms, along a playbook with several public implementations.

Caveat: the JVM Vector API (explicit SIMD) is intrinsified most completely by the stock C2 compiler; Graal's coverage has been partial. Within-core vectorization is the one line where a non-JVM backend keeps a clean advantage. Auto-vectorization is fragile on every JIT and should not be a design assumption.

## 2. GraalVM Native Image (cheap, orthogonal)

Closed-world ahead-of-time compilation of the existing Java+Scala toolchain into a standalone `fortress` binary with millisecond startup. It does not make programs faster; it makes the tool start instantly and ship as one file. Trades away dynamic class loading and some reflection, which the runtime instantiation of generics relies on, so feasibility needs a probe.

## 3. LLVM in the style of Julia (third era, only if the JVM is outgrown)

LLVM is only a code generator; Julia, Swift and Rust each wrote the other half themselves, and that other half is what the JVM gives Fortress for free: garbage collector, work-stealing runtime, exceptions, dynamic loading, and the STM behind `atomic`. Going native is a second implementation project. There is also a design collision: ahead-of-time generics mean choosing between monomorphization (Rust, whole-program) and uniform code with witness tables (Swift, works across module boundaries). Fortress's component/API system is a separate-compilation design, which pushes toward the Swift model and its performance cliffs, unless a JIT stays in the loop and specializes at run time, which is the Julia architecture. What it buys: ownership of object layout (flattened arrays of user types without waiting for Valhalla), LLVM's vectorizer and every SIMD ISA, cheap C/MPI/OpenMP interop, and cultural fit with the HPC venue Fortress was pitched at. Chapel, the surviving HPCS language, compiles natively.

## 4. MLIR as the missing middle (architecture, whichever backend)

MLIR's contribution is dialects: intermediate representations at the language's own abstraction level, lowered progressively. A `BIG` operator over a generator can stay an algebraic node subject to monoid-law rewrites, which is what licenses splitting it for parallelism, and only become loops at the end. That is the "compiler should see the algebra" story behind Fortress's generator/reducer library; in 2012 there was nowhere to put it, so it lives half-desugared in `FortressLibrary.fss`. Any serious new backend should have this layer, whether or not literal MLIR is underneath.

## Lessons from the neighbours

- Julia solved the symmetric-dispatch-plus-parametric-types problem by dropping modular static checking and specializing per call at run time on LLVM. Fortress kept the static checking; that is the unexplored quadrant.
- Swift ships unspecialized generics with run-time type metadata and specializes hot paths in the optimizer: the model Fortress reached for on the JVM, done with a compiler that owns the whole pipeline.
- Mojo restates Fortress's one-language-for-productivity-and-performance thesis for the GPU era with the opposite front-end bet: wrap the incumbent syntax and hide an MLIR-native language behind it. Swift for TensorFlow is the cautionary tale of a research language living on a patron's strategy.
- Scala and Kotlin grew native and JavaScript backends without changing their front ends; their JVM backends live with erased generics plus explicit or optimizer-driven specialization.
- The JVM itself has moved toward what Fortress needed (Project Valhalla: value classes, specialized generics); the exact status per JDK release must be checked before it is relied on.

## Sequencing

The front end survives every option, so nothing done in the modernization ladder forecloses any of them. A type-system map (which specified features are implemented, restricted, retracted or untested; see the not-working test directories under `ProjectFortress/` and the papers under `Papers/`) comes before any backend, because no backend rescues an unchecked ambiguity.

# The pure-Java microGPT: the baseline of P-7, and its timings

Paths are under `explorations/` unless they start with `Library/` or `ProjectFortress/`. "The flat program" is `run-c4/src/MicroGptFlat.fss` with its vocabulary `FlatArrays.fss` and its data `FlatData.fss`. Everything here is in `java-baseline/`; `./run.sh` there compiles into `/tmp` and runs each thing this report cites. Nothing of Fortress was built or run for this report.

## 1. What was built

| File | What it is |
|---|---|
| `MicroGptFlat.java` | the model: `MicroGptFlat.fss` line for line. Each method is named after the model's function (`rmsn`, `sm`, `rmsn_b`, `sm_b`, `step`, `adam`, `learningRate`, `matName`, ...) and cites its line; `step` has one statement per expression of lines 52 to 71, under a comment that quotes the line |
| `FlatArrays.java` | the vocabulary as plain loops over `double[]`: the products (`mul`, `mulT`, `addMulT`, `tMul`), the per-head planes (`headsMulT`, `headsMul`, `headsTMul`), the keys (`gatherAdd`, `onehotTMul`), and the four seams through which the model reaches every row loop and every sum (`forRange`, `dot`, `sum`, `max`) |
| `FlatData.java` | the loaders and the corpus: `FlatData.fss` declaration for declaration, `parseFloat` included |
| `MicroGptFlatQuick.java`, `MicroGptFlatCheck.java` | the 7 and the 40 checks of the two `.fss` files of those names |
| `Bench.java`, `run.sh`, `asm-count.py`, `Probes.java`, `DotU.java` | the timing harness, the script, and the small measurements of sections 4 to 7 |
| `variants/vector/FlatArrays.java`, `variants/forkjoin/FlatArrays.java` | two other vocabularies, measured beside the baseline; the model and the checks are compiled unchanged against each |

The flat program has 4,192 parameters in nine matrices inside one vector. The Java keeps that layout: a matrix is an offset into `double[] p`, a view of the Fortress (a transpose, a row, the per-head planes) is an index computation in a loop, and the gradient is written at the same offsets, which is the order of `flat` (`MicroGptFlat.fss:71`).

`python-comparison.md` beside this report is another worker's note, which timed this program beside the Python, NumPy and APL ones.

## 2. What it reproduces of the checks

`./run.sh` runs the five-step program, the quick check and the full check. Both checks read the same files as the Fortress checks (`apl/reference/dzaima/w/*.txt`, `apl/reference/dzaima/docs.txt`, `run-c/goldens/*`) by the same relative paths, assert the same values and use the same tolerances (loss and gradient 10^-12, finite differences 10^-8, loaders and the zero count 0).

    VERDICT: 7 PASS, 0 FAIL of 7 -- ALL PASS
    VERDICT: 40 PASS, 0 FAIL of 40 -- ALL PASS

The measured differences of the quick check's seven values:

| Check (`MicroGptFlatQuick.fss`) | Java | Reference | Difference | Tolerance |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| loader: max of P - P0 over 4192 | | | 0.0 | 0 |
| corpus rows 0..15 | | | 0.0 | 0 |
| batch 1 step 1 loss | 3.3659669475848517 | 3.365966947584851 | 8.9e-16 | 1e-12 |
| step 0 gradient, max over 4192 | | | 8.3e-17 | 1e-12 |
| zero gradient entries | 464 | 464 | 0 | 0 |
| P after Adam, max over 4192 | | | 1.9e-16 | 1e-12 |
| batch 1 step 2 loss | 3.4242727838717717 | 3.424272783871772 | 4.4e-16 | 1e-12 |

So the two losses agree with the references to 15 significant digits (the difference is at most 2 units in the last place of a double), and the gradient and the updated parameters to 1.9e-16 absolute. In the full check the five losses of batch 1, the batch-4 loss, the four single-document losses and the weighted mean differ from the references by at most 8.9e-16; the 22 finite-difference values differ from backpropagation by at most 5.2e-10 (tolerance 1e-8).

Walk's own run of the quick check prints `3.3659669475848513` and `3.424272783871772` for the two losses (`compile-ladder/plan-30/PROBES.md:29-30`, 2026-11-10). The Java differs from walk in the last digits: see section 3.

## 3. What could not be matched, and what was chosen

**The order of the sums longer than 16 terms, and only that.** Everything else the Java computes by the operations of the Fortress source in its order: a division stays a division (no reciprocal), no fused multiply-add, the masked attention entries and the padded rows are computed as the Fortress computes them, `10.0^(-5)` is the folded constant `1e-5` and `beta1^t` is `Math.pow`, as walk's native is (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/nativeHelpers/simpleDoubleArith.java:76-78`).

- The library's matrix product adds the terms of each element in ascending order of the summed index: `Matrix.mul` splits the summed dimension in sequence, and forks only the rows and the columns (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:3044-3102`). The Java's products add in the same order. Only the first term differs in form (the library stores it, the Java adds it to 0.0), which cannot change a value other than the sign of a zero.
- The library's `DOT`, `SUM` and `BIG MAX` are reductions over a range. A range of more than `grainSize` = 16 elements splits at a power-of-two boundary and joins the two results (`Library/RangeInternals.fss:20`, `:1310-1327`); at most 16 elements fold left to right from the identity (`:1365-1373`). In the model at batch 1 the only sums of more than 16 terms are the softmax over the 27 logits (`sm` on line 61), which the library adds as (16 terms) + (11 terms). The Java adds all 27 left to right. That is the last-digit difference from walk above. The fork/join variant of section 6 adds them as the library does.
- With more than one document in a batch, `SUM vm` and the loss's `DOT` are also longer than 16.

**The parser is ported, not replaced.** `FlatData.parseFloat` accumulates the mantissa digit by digit in a double and scales once, so it is not correctly rounded. `./run.sh parse`:

    4192 numbers, 699 differ from Double.parseDouble, the worst by 2.0 ulp

So 699 of the 4,192 initial parameters that the flat program trains from are not the doubles nearest to the decimal text of the weight files. The Java uses the same arithmetic, so that it starts from the same parameters; with `Double.parseDouble` it would start from other ones. The loader check passes at tolerance 0 either way, because it reads `P0.txt` through the same parser.

**Decisions.** No decision of the curator covers these; each says which reading was acted on.

1. *Same operations per element, sums left to right.* The alternative, reordering sums or replacing divisions where the tolerance holds, would be faster in places (section 5) and was not taken in the baseline, so that a ratio of compiled Fortress to this program measures the implementation and not a different arithmetic. The Vector API variant shows what one reordering buys.
2. *Dense, as the Fortress.* All 16 positions of every document are computed, and all 16 by 16 attention entries, also those that the mask sends to exactly 0. Skipping them is an algorithmic saving open to both programs alike.
3. *Storage reused.* One step's arrays are allocated once per batch size and reused, and `adam` updates `p`, `m` and `v` in place, where the Fortress makes new arrays and returns three new vectors. What this saves was not measured.
4. *Products read the weights in place.* `x w^T` is a dot product of two rows. A version that copied each transposed weight matrix first, so that the inner loop ran along rows of both operands, measured the same within noise in one fork (step 109 against 101 microseconds, taken at different loads) and was dropped.
5. *No lambdas.* The row bodies are anonymous classes. With lambdas the first step of a cold JVM took 30 ms instead of 5 ms (one run each), the cost of the first lambda's bootstrap.
6. *The model reaches loops and sums through four seams* (`forRange`, `dot`, `sum`, `max` in `FlatArrays`), so that the two variants replace the vocabulary alone. After warm-up the step measured the same with and without the seams (101.9 against 100.9 and 102.5 microseconds, one or two forks each).

## 4. Timings of the baseline

### Method

- Machine: 4 CPUs, Intel Xeon @ 2.30GHz (AVX-512), 15 GB, a cloud container shared with other sessions, which were building and running throughout. The load average is given with every run; it was never below 1.
- JDK: OpenJDK 25.0.4.1 (`/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64`, the JDK of `experiment/env.sh`), 64-bit server VM, mixed mode, class-data sharing on. Flags: none; `JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS` unset, as `env.sh` does. So: tiered compilation, G1, the default heap. The program has one thread; the JVM's compiler and collector threads run beside it on the other CPUs.
- In process, after warm-up (`Bench fork`): one fork is a fresh JVM. It loads the parameters, runs the three workloads below in turn for 4 s (2,600 to 3,000 rounds), then takes 30 samples of each, the workloads in turn so that a change of load reaches all three. A sample is the mean time of one call over a block of consecutive calls that fills about 20 ms (about 198 calls of `step1`, 35 of `train5`, 50 of `step4`), each call timed by `System.nanoTime` around it alone. Every loss and one element of the result are added to a sink. 10 forks. The harness prints the median of each fork's first and second half of samples; they agree within 3 microseconds for `step1` in every fork, so the warm-up had ended.
- Whole processes, cold: 30 runs of each program, the wall time from before the launch to after the exit, read from bash's `EPOCHREALTIME` around `java ... > /dev/null`. It includes the JVM's start, class loading, reading the corpus (2,000 lines) and the nine weight files, and for the checks the reference files.

## 6. Fork/join: the baseline in the shape of the library and the compiled runtime

`variants/forkjoin/FlatArrays.java` gives the vocabulary's loops and sums the shape that the Fortress library and its compiled runtime give parallel work, on a `java.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool`. What a piece computes once it is no longer split is the baseline's plain loop, so its time is a floor for what compiled Fortress could reach with this structure and unboxed arrays.

| Shape | In the tree | In the variant |
|---|---|---|
| a parallel range | `Library/RangeInternals.fss:1310-1345`: a range of more than `grainSize` = 16 elements (`:20`) splits at the highest power-of-two boundary inside it; the two parts are the arms of a `do ... also do` | `forRange`, used by the model's row loops (`rows(rmsn)`, `rows(sm)`, ...), by `adam`'s loop over the 4,192 elements, by the loop over the planes and by the elementwise passes |
| a reduction | the same split, the two results joined; at most 16 elements fold left to right (`:1365-1373`) | `dot`, `sum`, `max`: no shared accumulator |
| the matrix product | `Library/FortressLibrary.fss:3044-3102`: the largest of the three dimensions is halved by `partition` (the largest power of two below it); the halves of the rows and of the columns are forked, the halves of the summed dimension run in sequence; it stops at one element | `mma`, under `mul`, `mulT`, `addMulT`, `tMul` and on each plane under the three `heads*` |
| the arms | `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java:1717-1770` and `runtimeSystem/BaseTask.java`: every arm but the first becomes a task object; `forkIfProfitable` forks it if the pool has more than one thread and the worker's surplus of queued tasks is at most the spawn threshold (5, `FortressExecutable.java:26`); the first arm runs in place; `joinOrRun` joins the task or runs it in place | `Arm`: the same two methods; the program's body runs as a task of the pool |

Not given the shape: `gatherAdd`, `onehotTMul`, `addInto` and the elementwise loops written in `step` itself stay plain loops, and `onehotTMul` stays a scatter where the Fortress multiplies by a 0/1 matrix.

**Grains.** `baseline.grain` is the range's grain and `baseline.mmgrain` the product's: a product whose three dimensions are all at most that is one plain block. The library's own are 16 for the range and 1 for the product, which has no grain: it forks down to single elements. Timed: the library's (16, 1); (16, 16), the product given the range's grain, at which a 16x16x16 product is one block and only the 27 and 64 dimensions split; and (4, 4), finer, at which the model's sizes do split.

**The order of the sums against the plain loop.** The product's halving does not change it at any grain: the summed dimension is split in sequence. The range's halving changes every sum longer than the grain: at grain 16 the softmax sum over 27 logits, as in the library; at grain 4 every sum of 16 as well. Every configuration passes the 7 and the 40 checks (`./run.sh variants`: 9 configurations, threads 1, 2, 4 by the three grains). `compile-ladder/plan-31/probes/switch-rehearsal.md`, section 5, gives the first compiled Fortress program with an array that ran against the interpreter's library: `DotU`, two arrays of 1,000 `RR64` and the loop `s += a[i] b[i]` over them run 5,000 times, 5 million iterations. `DotU.java` is that loop in plain Java with `double[]`, the same sizes and count; the rehearsal's source is not in the tree, so the fill (`a[i] = i`, `b[i] = 1.0`) is the one that gives its printed values, and it prints the same `total = 2.4975E9`. `./run.sh dot`, load 2.0 before and 1.9 after:

| What | Time |
|---|---|
| Fortress under walk, whole process (the rehearsal's one timing) | 39.8 s |
| Fortress compiled against the one library, whole process, the verifier off (the rehearsal's one timing) | 1.4 s |
| Java, whole process, 30 runs | median 44.3 ms (quartiles 42.5 to 46.6, min 40.0, max 53.5) |
| Java, the loops' own time in a cold JVM, 30 runs | median 7.47 ms (7.04 to 8.76) |
| Java, in process after 2 s of warm-up, 5 forks of 30 samples | fork medians 4.37 to 4.50 ms (min 4.23), 0.87 ns per iteration |

The two Fortress numbers are another worker's single timing, in another session, at another load (3.7 to 4.8), not taken with the Java's. That report puts a one-line program at 0.6 s compiled and 3.8 s under walk, so about 0.8 s and 36 s for the loop. Against the Java's cold loop of 7.5 ms that is of the order of 100 times for compiled Fortress and of 5,000 times for walk; as whole processes, of the order of 30 and 900 times. These are orders of magnitude and no more.

## 8. The lines of the Fortress that were hardest to read as an algorithm

- `MicroGptFlat.fss:59`, `a = rows(sm, mask + (qh kh^T) / SQRT (1.0 headDim)); hc = u(a vh)`. Three things on it are not visible from the line: the juxtaposition of two rank-3 arrays is a product on every pair of planes (`FlatArrays.fss:127`), `^T` on a rank-3 array transposes every plane (`MicroGptFlat.fss:24`), and `mask +` adds one matrix to every plane (`FlatArrays.fss:135`). Every operand has the type `Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32)\]`, so no shape is on the page; the shapes had to be worked out from `heads` (`FlatArrays.fss:84-96`), whose index arithmetic `(q DIV nh) p + i, (q MOD nh) k + j` is itself juxtaposition for multiplication between integer names.
- `MicroGptFlat.fss:66`, `dS = rows(sm_b, a, dh vh^T) / SQRT (1.0 headDim)`: which of the four `rows` it is (the one over two rank-3 arrays), and that `dh vh^T` groups as `dh (vh^T)`.
- `MicroGptFlat.fss:63`, `diag(vm / nv) (pr - onehot(tg, vocabSize))`: a juxtaposition of a diagonal object and a matrix that scales the rows; `MicroGptFlat.fss:70`, a scatter-add written as a product with a transposed 0/1 matrix.
- `MicroGptFlat.fss:32`, `(dy - y ((y DOT dy) / |y|)) / r`: `y (...)` reads as an application and is a scaling; `|y|` is the number of elements, not a norm.
- The order in which a sum is added is on no line of the model. It took the library's `Matrix.mul`, `Vector.dot` and the range's `generate` to learn that a product adds in sequence and a dot product over more than 16 elements does not.
- `MicroGptFlat.fss:18`, `10.0^(-5)`: whether it is `Math.pow` at run time or a folded constant decides the last bit of `epsilon`; the skill's rule on numerals settles it (folded).

## 9. For the record

**Defects.** None found in the tree. One property of the model's data path that the record may want as a fact: `FlatData.parseFloat` is not correctly rounded (section 3); no check depends on it.

**Sentences of the specification made false.** None: nothing outside this folder changed, except one line of `coordinator/INDEX.md`.

**Points to report.** The brief named none beyond the final message's items.

**For FACTS** (the brief did not let this work write FACTS):

1. A pure-Java microGPT, the baseline that P-7 names, is in `java-baseline/` and passes the flat program's 7 quick and 40 full checks at their tolerances; one step at batch 1 takes about 0.10 ms after warm-up on this machine (fork medians 100.8 to 104.0 microseconds, 10 forks, 2026-11-10), the five-step run 72 ms and the quick check 77 ms as cold processes (medians of 30). Meaning: the distance of compiled microGPT to Java can be measured as soon as the flat program compiles. Shown by `java-baseline/run.sh` and `run.sh bench`; detail in sections 2 and 4.
2. The baseline's hot loops are scalar: HotSpot's C2 in OpenJDK 25 vectorises none of its matrix products, and the Vector API in the products alone brings the step from 101 to 75 microseconds. Meaning: the baseline is the careful scalar Java, not the fastest Java. Shown by `run.sh asm` and `run.sh steps`; detail in section 5.
3. In the fork/join shape of the library and the compiled runtime, with unboxed arrays and plain loops at the leaves, the model's step is 19 to 80 times slower than the plain loop at the library's grains (16 for a range, 1 for the matrix product) and 1.4 to 4.8 times slower with the product's grain at 16; threads gain only from products of about 128 by 128. Meaning: at microGPT's sizes the library's parallel shape costs time at any thread count, and the matrix product's missing grain is the largest part of it. Shown by `run.sh steps`, `run.sh kernels`, `run.sh scale`; detail in section 6.
4. 699 of the 4,192 parameters that `FlatData.parseFloat` reads differ from the nearest double of their text, by up to 2 ulp. Meaning: a port of the model must port the parser to start from the same parameters. Shown by `java-baseline/run.sh parse`; detail in section 3.

**Commands.** `java-baseline/run.sh` with no argument runs the three programs; `quick`, `check`, `run` one of them; `bench [forks] [processes]` section 4; `asm`, `kernels [forks]`, `steps [forks]`, `scale`, `axpy` sections 5 and 6; `variants` every check on both variants; `dot` section 7; `parse` section 3. To read machine code without `hsdis`: `java -XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions -XX:CompileCommand=print,Class::method ... | java-baseline/asm-count.py`.

**Questions for the curator.** One decision not taken: whether the baseline that P-7 names is this scalar program or the fastest Java that keeps the checks. Acted on: the scalar program, as the brief says ("the one-thread plain-loop program stays the baseline"), with the Vector API variant measured beside it.
